newsitem.title: USA: New Avis chief rejects discrimination charges.
newsitem.headline: New Avis chief rejects discrimination charges.

text.p: The new chief executive of Avis Rent-A-Car on Monday pledged "zero tolerance" for any illegal discrimination by any Avis employee, but reiterated the company's position that recent allegations are untrue.
R. Craig Hoenshell made his comments in a statement released by Avis after he did not appear as scheduled at a New York public hearing on alleged discrimination by rental car companies.
Avis is a unit of HFS Inc. HFS shares closed down 2-3/8 to 58-7/8 on Monday.
Hoenshell was named chairman and chief executive of the car-rental unit two weeks ago.

Hoenshell said in his statement he decided not to appear at the hearing because it seemed that its focus had shifted from a proposed new law to pending litigation against Avis, which it would be inappropriate for him to discuss.

New York State Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, a Manhattan Democrat, co-presided at the hearing, at which a former Avis employee claimed Avis facilities at LaGuardia and Newark airports tended to be more suspicious of non-white people who wanted to rent cars.
"If they were non-Caucasian, they were screened harder," the former employee, Derek Knowlin, testified.
John Carley, Avis executive vice president and general counsel, later told Reuters that Avis had no knowledge of any evidence that would back up Knowlin's charges.
"Avis emphatically denies any such practice or policy ever existed," he said. "We rent to lots of people at LaGuardia, many of whom are minorities."

Avis faces a lawsuit filed in Florida alleging that some of its employees discriminated against a Jewish man and another lawsuit in North Carolina that claims an Avis franchisee there discriminated against blacks.
Silver has filed a proposed bill that would require car-rental companies in New York to be licensed as part of an effort to prevent discrimination.
"Discrimination is not and can never be a risk-management strategy," Silver said at the hearing in Manhattan.
The proposed law was strongly opposed at the hearing by independent franchisees, who said they fear it will add to the pressures that could drive many of them out of business.
